floor_changes.why: More flats get a square-on river view.

rows.reason: The rotating triangle has character that fits a cluster of glass slabs. Truncating the corners fixes most of the efficiency penalty.
rows.quote: Fix the tips of A and it earns its place. B is just another box on the Isle of Dogs.

det.whats_wrong: A triangular plate that rotates about 90 degrees over the height. The idea is Heatherwick-like and the silhouette is clear. But triangles give awkward acute corners, which cost plan efficiency. The top of the rotation turns a point, not a face, toward the docks, so the rotation does little for the view.

floor_changes.why: Usable corner rooms instead of wasted acute tips.

floor_changes.direction: hold a broad face toward the Thames and docks to the north
floor_changes.why: The upper, most valuable floors face the water squarely.

prob.whats_wrong: A rotated square extruded straight up: efficient and repeatable. It is dull next to the Canary Wharf cluster and does nothing to reach toward the river to the north.

floor_changes.why: Gives a softer top and less bulk facing the lower housing to the south.

rows.reason: A's slenderness and simple plate fit my priorities. B is heavy and gives away the height that would buy the sea view.
rows.quote: A has the right proportion. Now cut some gardens into it.

det.whats_wrong: A slender rotated square rising straight to 180 m. The proportion is good and so is repetition. Its diagonal orientation puts corners, not faces, toward the sea to the north-west and the park to the east. None of the Safdie-style gardens Mumbai's climate calls for.

floor_changes.direction: at the north-west and east corners
floor_changes.why: Shaded sky gardens that face the sea and the park.
A more refined, Piano-style finish to the top.

prob.whats_wrong: A stout chamfered octagon only about 115 m tall, with slab edges that step. That adds texture, but the tower is squat, uses less than half the permitted height and looks bulky beside the park.

floor_changes.why: Better proportion, and more flats get the corner outlook.
Uses the permitted height to reach views of the sea.

rows.reason: The twist is expressive and turns the long face toward the water as the tower rises.
rows.quote: A is at least trying to move. B just stands there in the canyon.

det.whats_wrong: A rectangular slab that turns about 50 degrees as it rises. The twist gives the flowing, MAD-like quality I want and gradually swings the long face toward the harbour. But the lower floors are hemmed in by towers close by, and the glass is unshaded on the south-west faces.

floor_changes.why: Lets in light and opens the view up the canyon for the lowest flats.

floor_changes.direction: toward the harbour to the south-west
floor_changes.why: Aims the long face of the top floors fully at the water.
Shades the glass that faces the sun.

prob.whats_wrong: A static chamfered hexagon at every level. It is stiff and closed, it ignores the harbour, and neighbouring towers look straight in.

floor_changes.direction: toward the harbour to the south
floor_changes.why: Brings some movement and reaches toward the view.

rows.reason: B is more slender; A has the better plate for flats. In Midtown the neighbours dominate either way.
rows.quote: In a canyon like this, the twist is decoration. Get above the neighbours first.

det.whats_wrong: A rectangular plate that rotates about 40 degrees over 40 floors. In Midtown the aerial from the outlook side is filled by a huge neighbouring tower, so the lower two thirds face walls. The rotation adds cost without clearly buying a view.

floor_changes.direction: hold the plate square to the grid
floor_changes.why: The views are blocked here anyway, so repetition is worth more.

floor_changes.direction: long face toward the park to the east
floor_changes.why: Aims the flats that clear the neighbours at the open square.

prob.whats_wrong: A smaller square plate that twists steadily. It is more slender than A, but the twist has the same problem: it spends effort on floors hemmed in by towers. The square plate gives less facade length per flat.

floor_changes.amount: use the full 150 m, adding about 2 floors
floor_changes.why: Gets more of the building above the canyon.
More distance from the facade opposite.

rows.reason: A's articulated slab edges start to give a climate and skyline response. B is inert.
rows.quote: A has the start of an idea. Now make the edges shade something.

prob.whats_wrong: Two chamfered towers with faceted, slightly wavy slab edges: a hint of Zaha-like movement. They sit close together on a diagonal, so each overlooks the other. There is no shading response, and the base gives nothing to the street.

floor_changes.why: Gives shade and public realm on a hot Manhattan street.

floor_changes.direction: rotate the flats that face each other outward
floor_changes.why: Stops the flats in the two towers looking into each other.
Shading, verandah-style.

det.whats_wrong: Two small square extrusions with identical plates. They are easy to build, but mute and slab-like, and they offer no shading or public ground.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Hudson to the west
floor_changes.why: Gives the upper flats outdoor rooms and a view.

rows.reason: A has fair views for everyone but wastes the site. B has more flats, but the southern tower is sacrificed.
rows.quote: One of B's towers is looking at the back of the other. That is not a view, that is a punishment.

det.whats_wrong: One slim rotated-square tower on a site asked for three. It is honest and gives every flat light on four sides. But it makes no gesture toward the park to the north or the sea to the west, and it wastes the site.

floor_changes.direction: a flat face toward Shivaji Park and the sea to the north-west
floor_changes.why: Every flat, not only the corners, then shares the park and sea view.

prob.whats_wrong: Two rounded towers stacked one behind the other on a north-south line. The southern tower's northern view, the park view, is blocked by its twin: bad view equity. The rounded plates are fine.

floor_changes.why: Unblocks the southern tower's view to the park and the sea.
Lets the southern tower see over it to the sea.

rows.reason: A has the slenderness and discipline a Midtown pencil tower needs, and it can be built. B's wobble costs money and gives away height.
rows.quote: In Midtown, slenderness is the product. Don't blur it with wobbles.

det.whats_wrong: A pure diamond pencil to 274 m reads cleanly among the Midtown supertalls, and it is admirably slender. But the plate is identical at every level, so the lower 20 floors put their corner flats straight into neighbouring slabs. The base does nothing for the street: it just drops a rotated square into a large, empty envelope.

floor_changes.amount: 4-storey street wall filling the envelope edge, set back 3 m for an arcade
floor_changes.why: Hold the Manhattan street wall and give the public realm something back.

floor_changes.direction: sharpest corner toward the river gap to the west
floor_changes.why: Aim the corner flats down the cross-street canyon instead of at the neighbouring slab.

floor_changes.amount: open double-height mechanical and amenity breaks every 12 floors, crown recessed 2 m
floor_changes.why: Wind relief and a finished top, in the manner of 432 Park.

prob.whats_wrong: The chamfered square wobbles from floor to floor. It pinches at mid-height and swells again at the top, and the stacked slabs look fussy rather than elegant. At 241 m it is also shorter, so it wastes allowable height that Midtown pays for. The base sits well against the park to the south-east, which is a plus.

floor_changes.amount: no more than 2 plate variants in total
floor_changes.why: The random plate drift costs formwork and adds nothing visible from the street.

floor_changes.amount: add about 35 m to reach the 280 m allowance
floor_changes.why: The premium floors above the neighbouring towers are where the value lies.

floor_changes.direction: toward the park to the SE
floor_changes.why: Park-facing terraces sell and soften the base.

rows.reason: B keeps the repetition but turns its corners toward the water.
rows.quote: Same formwork, better corners, so I take B.

det.whats_wrong: An efficient square extrusion that builds easily. But the tower sits deep among taller neighbours, the flat faces look directly at the towers opposite, and nothing turns toward the harbour visible to the north-east.

floor_changes.direction: toward the East River to the NE
floor_changes.why: Slips the windows past the neighbouring tower faces.

floor_changes.amount: one 4 x 4 m loggia per floor
floor_changes.why: Gives corner flats an outlook to the water above the neighbouring roofs.

prob.whats_wrong: The chamfered, slightly rotated octagon is the better-oriented plate. The chamfer corners give diagonal views. It is still a constant extrusion, and at 184 m it stops short of the neighbouring crowns.

floor_changes.why: Bigger chamfers mean wider diagonal glazing toward the harbour at little cost.

floor_changes.amount: about 6 m to use the full 190 m
floor_changes.why: Clears the neighbouring roofline.

rows.reason: A's plan is more efficient and it faces the river better.
rows.quote: The octagon is kind to the plan and kind to the river.

prob.whats_wrong: The octagonal plate works well: it faces the Thames bend to the north and slides past the heavy slab to the south-east. It is modest in height against the cluster, and the ground plane is just a leftover polygon of hardstanding.

floor_changes.amount: a shaded open-to-sky forecourt of about 400 m²
floor_changes.why: Correa's lesson: the ground is a room, not residue.

floor_changes.amount: double-height sky garden, one per band
floor_changes.why: Breaks the extrusion and gives the river a communal terrace.

det.whats_wrong: A diamond with a few clipped corners. The acute corners cut up the plan and are hard to furnish. Its broad faces look east and west into the cluster rather than north to the river.

floor_changes.direction: a flat face toward the Thames to the N
floor_changes.why: A full frontage on the water rather than a point.
Makes the plan usable.

rows.reason: B respects the two-tower limit and gives each flat air and a view.
rows.quote: Two towers that breathe beat three that stare at one another.

prob.whats_wrong: Three octagonal towers are crammed onto a plot that can only take two properly. Their windows look into one another across short gaps, and they overwhelm the chawl-scale fabric around Shivaji Park.

floor_changes.why: Restores the separation distances and the privacy.

floor_changes.amount: a stilted open ground floor with a shaded courtyard
floor_changes.why: A Correa-style open-to-sky space for the monsoon.

det.whats_wrong: Two well-spaced slabs, rotated to face the park and the sea. They are still plain extrusions with no verandahs, nothing to shade the western sun, and no step down toward the low-rise edge.

floor_changes.direction: west faces toward the Arabian Sea
floor_changes.amount: 2.4 m deep verandahs on alternate floors
floor_changes.why: Shade, cross-ventilation and sea views.

floor_changes.direction: toward Shivaji Park to the NW
floor_changes.why: Meets the scale of the park edge.

floor_changes.direction: east tower turned away from the west tower
floor_changes.why: Stops the two towers looking straight at each other.

rows.reason: The longer frontage to the water is the better starting point for a sculpted form.
rows.quote: B has the bones. Now give it a crown worth seeing from the ferry.

prob.whats_wrong: A static diamond prism. The acute corner points to the water but gives no identity on the skyline and no shading response. It reads as a stick among the harbour towers.

floor_changes.why: Gives the skyline a sculpted top.

floor_changes.amount: 1.2 m deep fins or recessed balconies
floor_changes.why: Shading for the western sun.

det.whats_wrong: The rotated bar gives a longer frontage toward the river, which is right. But its flat top and unarticulated faces waste the waterfront skyline moment.

floor_changes.amount: a sloping crown that drops 12 m toward the water
floor_changes.why: A skyline signature.
Sculptural form plus better harbour views higher up.
Solar control.

rows.reason: A's chamfers and drift give more flats a way to look past their neighbours.
rows.quote: A small turn, but every flat deserves it.

prob.whats_wrong: The chamfered plate drifts gently, which is pleasant, but the flats at the base look straight into the massive block to the south-west. Not every flat gets a fair view, because half of each floor faces that wall.

floor_changes.direction: away from the big block to the SW
floor_changes.why: Increases the privacy distance.

floor_changes.direction: toward the river glimpses to the E
floor_changes.why: Shares the view equally among the flats.
A privacy buffer.

det.whats_wrong: A plain square box. Its flat faces look into the neighbours, so view equity is poor and the building has no character.

floor_changes.why: Diagonal views that avoid the facing walls.

floor_changes.direction: alternating to the E and N
floor_changes.why: Varies the outlook and privacy for every flat.

rows.reason: The river orientation and height are worth it, provided the twist is rationalised into steps.
rows.quote: The data says height and the river win. Just discretise the twist.

prob.whats_wrong: The square twists about 40 degrees on the triangular site, and the upper floors come to face the Thames better. But every plate is different, which is costly, and the lower floors sit tight against the heavy neighbours to the east.

floor_changes.amount: stepped rotation in 4 blocks of about 10 degrees each
floor_changes.why: Keeps the orientation benefit with repeatable floors.

floor_changes.direction: away from the tower to the E
floor_changes.why: Privacy at the lower floors.

det.whats_wrong: A repeatable rotated rectangle, very buildable, and it follows the long axis of the site. At 144 m it wastes about 70 m of allowable height, and the lower floors are hidden behind the neighbours. It faces the river diagonally at best.

floor_changes.why: The river views begin above the neighbouring roofs.

floor_changes.direction: a long face toward the Thames to the S
floor_changes.why: A full river frontage.

rows.reason: B is more slender and better turned toward the river.
rows.quote: Keep the facets, lose the jitter, and it becomes a fine tower.

det.whats_wrong: A flat-faced rectangular slab. Its long face is broadside to the sun and the tower is visually heavy. There is no shading and it ignores the Thames to the south.

floor_changes.why: A more elegant proportion.
Shading in the Piano manner.

prob.whats_wrong: The faceted octagon stands tall and clear, with the river open beyond. But the stacked floor-to-floor wobble is nervous where it should be calm.

floor_changes.amount: replace the random drift with a single gentle taper
floor_changes.why: Calm, slender elegance.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Thames to the S
floor_changes.why: Lightens the top and opens river views.

rows.reason: B has a skyline presence befitting the site, with water views that shift as the floors rise.
rows.quote: B has a silhouette. Chamfer its corners and it will be a landmark.

prob.whats_wrong: A slender chamfered square with a slight taper, on a riverside site with unobstructed water. It is elegant but anonymous for a 288 m waterfront landmark, and there are no verandah-like spaces.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Hudson to the W
floor_changes.amount: a stepped crown cut back 3 m per 3 floors
floor_changes.why: Skyline identity.
Doshi-like shaded outdoor rooms facing the water.

det.whats_wrong: The triangular plate twists about 90 degrees, a strong sculptural gesture, and the faces sweep toward the water as they rise. But the acute corners are hard to plan, and the twist raises cost at every floor.

floor_changes.why: Usable corner rooms and better wind behaviour.
A more slender top.
Constructability, while keeping the identity.

rows.reason: The plate changes as it rises, so the form is responding to something. A is a plain extrusion.
rows.quote: B at least measures its site. A just repeats one floor 39 times.

prob.whats_wrong: A small square plate, rotated 45 degrees and extruded straight up. It sits hard against the big curved tower to its east, so the corners facing the Thames to the south look straight into that tower. The stepped bands on the facade give some shade, but nothing is orientated for the south sun or the river.

floor_changes.direction: long face toward the Thames to the S/SW, away from the curved tower to the E
floor_changes.why: stops the lower flats looking straight into the neighbour's glass
the terraces act as deep shading overhangs and open river views above the cluster

det.whats_wrong: The chamfer that grows up the SE side is a start: the plate thins toward the top. But the cut is on the wrong side for shade, because it opens the flats to the hot SE sun and puts no depth in front of that glass. The east side still crowds the neighbouring tower.

floor_changes.direction: keep the cut SE but add deep fins facing SW
floor_changes.why: cuts solar gain while keeping the angle toward the river
slimmer proportion to set against the cluster

rows.reason: A wins on plan efficiency and B wins on views. The right answer is a stepped twist that sits between them.
rows.quote: A twist that changes every floor is a cost plan with a nice render on top.

prob.whats_wrong: Very efficient repetition: the plate is almost identical at every level and sits slightly off the grid. But in Midtown a plain box gets no view past its neighbours below about 100 m, and nothing on the plate is aimed toward the park to the north.

floor_changes.direction: toward the park to the N
floor_changes.amount: about 10 degrees, done once in a single transfer floor
floor_changes.why: captures the park view and keeps the repetitive floors below it

det.whats_wrong: A continuous twist of about 50 degrees on a rectangular plate. It opens diagonal views, but every floor is different, so there is little repetition. The columns shift at every level, and the corner flats lose efficiency.

floor_changes.direction: rotate in steps toward the park to the N
floor_changes.amount: 3 steps of 15 degrees, each held for about 15 floors
floor_changes.why: about 80% of the view gain while keeping repeatable floor zones

rows.reason: There is more sellable area on repeatable floors. The overlooking can be fixed by splaying the towers.
rows.quote: Three towers pay for the land. Just stop them staring at each other.

det.whats_wrong: A single very slender square tower on the edge of Shivaji Park. It is clean to build and nothing overlooks it, but it gives nothing back to the park or the low-rise Dadar fabric around it. It is also a lot of height to sell on one core.

floor_changes.why: matches the eaves line of the art-deco blocks that ring the park

floor_changes.direction: toward the Arabian Sea to the W
floor_changes.why: the premium sea view is worth more than the plain square

prob.whats_wrong: Three identical towers is good commercial repetition. But the two southern towers look across at each other, and the north tower blocks the sea view of the tower behind it. From the park the three read as a wall.

floor_changes.direction: turn the SW and middle towers apart, toward the sea to the W and the park to the S
floor_changes.why: stops the flats facing straight into each other
opens a sea view for the towers behind it and breaks up the wall

rows.reason: At least A's plan can be let. B's twin tubes are inefficient and overlook each other.
rows.quote: Two pencils with nothing to say. Give me one tower with a top.

det.whats_wrong: A diamond-shaped extrusion, 288 m tall, with no identity at all. It sits by the harbour and does nothing with it, and the top is flat.

floor_changes.direction: lift the crown toward the harbour to the S
floor_changes.why: a tower on this skyline needs a top
gives the shaft a silhouette

prob.whats_wrong: Two identical rounded tubes, too thin to plan well. They stand about 20 m apart and their flats face each other. Twin towers with no dialogue between them.

floor_changes.amount: one plate of about twice the area
floor_changes.why: a workable plan and a single strong form

floor_changes.direction: if both towers stay, lean them apart toward the East River and the harbour
floor_changes.why: privacy and a gesture on the skyline

rows.reason: B's proportion is closer to a slender Manhattan tower.
rows.quote: On a plot this small, you win the view by going up, not out.

det.whats_wrong: The plate is too big for the site, so the tower comes out squat at about 115 m against a 295 m allowance. The gentle rotation helps, but the lower floors look straight into the slab next door, which puts the view equity in the low flats at risk.

floor_changes.amount: about 25% less area, with the lost area moved upward
floor_changes.why: a slender proportion and more flats above the neighbours

floor_changes.direction: stack boxes pushed toward the park to the E
floor_changes.why: an MVRDV-style stack that gives every flat its own view

prob.whats_wrong: A square set on the diagonal and taller, which gives better proportion. But it is still a plain extrusion, and the corners give some flats the view while others get walls.

floor_changes.direction: on the corners facing the neighbours
floor_changes.why: light and privacy for the flats that lose out
use the height allowance for slenderness

rows.reason: The chamfers make the form friendlier with no loss of repeatability.
rows.quote: Lovely and buildable, but tell me which way the river is.

det.whats_wrong: A clean, repeatable rectangle with a slender shaft, and it stands clear of its neighbours. But the long faces run NW-SE, so neither faces Tower Bridge and the river to the south directly. It stands next to the Tower of London, and it does not respond to that.

floor_changes.direction: long face toward the Thames and Tower Bridge to the S
floor_changes.why: frames the river view

floor_changes.direction: toward the Tower to the S
floor_changes.why: respects the heritage setting

prob.whats_wrong: An octagon repeated all the way up. The chamfered corners spread the views more evenly and reduce wind, but the plan is still undirected: it does not choose the river.

floor_changes.why: private outdoor rooms facing the view, screened from the City to the north

rows.reason: B turns toward the water with a calm gesture.
rows.quote: The tower turns to the water like a person turning to the breeze.

prob.whats_wrong: A diamond plate that shifts slightly near the top, with horizontal bands. It is honest and repeatable, but there are no verandahs or shaded voids, and the face toward the dock water to the north is flat.

floor_changes.direction: on the N corner facing the docks and on the S corner
floor_changes.amount: a two-storey sky verandah every 5 floors
floor_changes.why: shaded outdoor rooms, as in Doshi's verandahs, framing the water

det.whats_wrong: A gentle twist of about 25 degrees gives the shaft grace and turns the upper floors toward the water. But the cost is a changing structure, and the upper plate grows slightly.

floor_changes.direction: hold the rotation reached at floor 22, facing the docks
floor_changes.why: Foster-style repetition above the turn
a finer top

rows.reason: The cruciform self-shades and gives corner outlook, and the loggias fix its privacy problem.
rows.quote: The cross shades itself. Now screen the inside corners.

prob.whats_wrong: A square box with a subtle twist. It stands right beside the slab to its west, so the west face gets both afternoon sun and overlooking, and there is no shading depth on the facade.

floor_changes.direction: away from the slab to the W, toward the Thames to the S
floor_changes.why: privacy from the slab
shading and screening against the low afternoon sun

det.whats_wrong: A cruciform plate whose arms give corner views and self-shade their re-entrant corners, which is good. But the recesses let flats look into each other across the corners, and the crown shifts at the top without a reason.

floor_changes.direction: fill the re-entrant corners with screened loggias
floor_changes.why: blocks flats looking into each other across the corners and adds shade

rows.reason: Softer corners and a more tactile shaft. It is closer to a humane tower.
rows.quote: A tower should begin at the pavement, and both of these forgot to.

det.whats_wrong: A very slender square set on the diagonal, which is nice. But it meets the street as a bare shaft and gives nothing to the public realm. Up the shaft, the diagonal corners point straight at the supertall next door.

floor_changes.why: gives space back to the street

floor_changes.direction: toward the river to the N, away from the supertall
floor_changes.why: privacy and a river view

prob.whats_wrong: The chamfered octagon has stacked setbacks that read well, and the softer corners help privacy. But the base still just meets the ground.

floor_changes.amount: a planted public terrace at level 6
floor_changes.why: a Heatherwick-like gift to the street
views that are screened from the sides

rows.reason: The two are practically the same object. Neither responds to the dock, the slab to the east or the street.
rows.quote: Two identical sticks. The site is asking for a gesture to the water and a proper ground floor, and neither gives it one.

prob.whats_wrong: A diamond-set square prism, dead straight for 32 floors, sitting in the shadow of the big slab to its east. Setting the plate on the diagonal points the corners at the docks, which is right, but nothing in the section changes and the podium does nothing for the dockside. The west face looks straight at the drum tower.

floor_changes.direction: toward the dock edge to the north-west
floor_changes.amount: pull the base back 4-6 m to open a colonnade
floor_changes.why: give the dockside walk a public threshold

floor_changes.direction: toward the river and docks to the NW
floor_changes.why: get out of the slab's shadow and aim the long face at the water
a finer crown that reads against the Canary Wharf cluster

det.whats_wrong: Almost identical to A. The plate starts slightly smaller and swells mid-height, then shrinks again, which gives no gain you can read in the image. Same shadowed eastern flank, same inert base.

floor_changes.amount: a double-height loggia about 8 m deep
floor_changes.why: it is the public realm that makes this tower belong
more sky between it and the slab to the east

floor_changes.direction: toward the water to the NW
floor_changes.why: clear the neighbour and give the upper flats the dock

rows.reason: A's twist at least tries to turn the faces away from one another. B is tidier but indifferent to where the flats look.
rows.quote: The twist is the right instinct; the fourth tower is the wrong one.

det.whats_wrong: Four rectangular slabs that rotate progressively with height. The twist is elegant and splays the faces, but the central tower sits inside the ring of the other three, so every flat on it looks into a neighbour at around 25-30 m. Four towers at this density crowd the medieval grain.

floor_changes.why: view equity: the middle block has no outlook of its own

floor_changes.direction: turn the outer long faces outward, away from the centre
floor_changes.why: stop the living rooms facing one another
Doshi-style shaded ground that cools the space between the towers

prob.whats_wrong: Chamfered octagonal plates that taper gently. The chamfers are calmer in the City and soften the corner-to-corner views, but the faces point nowhere in particular, and the central tower still overlooks everything.

floor_changes.direction: push the central tower toward the NE edge
floor_changes.why: open a gap to the south toward the Thames
give every flat a slice of the river
stepping gives outdoor space and fairer views

rows.reason: The chamfered corners of A give the harbour a better reading. Both suffer from the same stacking problem.
rows.quote: On the evidence, the north tower gets the harbour and the south tower gets a wall. Offset them.

prob.whats_wrong: Two chamfered square towers stacked north to south with only a modest gap. The north tower looks straight onto the harbour and park, but the south tower sits behind it and looks into its back. There is no shading response on the south and west façades.

floor_changes.why: a diagonal offset opens a harbour view past the north tower
let the rear tower see over it toward the water
Correa-style deep shade on the hot façades

det.whats_wrong: Plain square extrusions in the same stacked arrangement. They are the most buildable, but the sharp corners and dead-straight sides read as generic in a district that is full of setbacks and heritage crowns.

floor_changes.amount: setbacks of 3 m at two levels
floor_changes.why: answer the setback tradition of Lower Manhattan
wider panoramic corners and less wind
break the face-to-face stacking

rows.reason: B's rounded plate is more saleable and more private. It should use the full height allowance.
rows.quote: B sells better, but give me the podium and the extra 40 metres.

prob.whats_wrong: A very slender square pencil rising to about 266 m. The height buys views over Midtown, but it is a generic stick with no street base, and the lower third looks straight into the office slab next door.

floor_changes.why: hold the Midtown streetwall and give retail frontage
a crown sells the penthouses and joins the skyline

floor_changes.direction: away from the slab to the south-east
floor_changes.why: lower flats avoid looking straight at the neighbour

det.whats_wrong: A rounded squircle that tapers slightly to about 223 m. It is softer and more marketable, and the rounded corners blur the sightlines between neighbours, but it is lower and still has no podium engaging the street.

floor_changes.why: street and heritage context

floor_changes.amount: about 40 m, to the allowed height
floor_changes.why: penthouse premium above the neighbours
a clean finish on the skyline

rows.reason: The twist in B creates the ledges that can become terraces. A is inert.
rows.quote: B has the bones for balconies; A is a filing cabinet.

prob.whats_wrong: A straight square prism rotated off the grid. It is very buildable, but it has no outdoor space and does nothing about St Paul's or the medieval grain. It is a generic extrusion on a tricky site.

floor_changes.why: balconies for every flat and a stepped face to the river
shaded outdoor rooms in Doshi's manner

floor_changes.direction: away from St Paul's to the west
floor_changes.why: soften the silhouette against the dome

det.whats_wrong: A rectangular plate that twists roughly 40 degrees up the height, turning from the diagonal toward north-south. It gives more variety and the twisted steps leave small ledges, but the slab is broad and the ledges are too small to be usable terraces.

floor_changes.amount: make them 2.5 m deep usable terraces
floor_changes.why: outdoor space per flat

floor_changes.direction: stop with the long face toward the Thames
floor_changes.why: lock the upper flats onto the river
a slimmer slab next to the heritage views

rows.reason: B has a real silhouette and a prow that aims at gaps in the cluster, and it will panelise more cleanly than A's stepped rotation.
rows.quote: The triangle's got attitude. Chop the tips and it's buildable.

prob.whats_wrong: A square plate that rotates in increments with visible stepped ledges. The stepping is a nice move for the façade, but the stagger complicates the curtain wall, and the tower is boxed in by the drum tower and slabs on the Thames side.

floor_changes.amount: rotate in 5-floor blocks rather than every floor
floor_changes.why: repeated mullion modules and fewer unique corner panels

floor_changes.direction: toward the Thames to the NW
floor_changes.amount: end with a face square to the river

floor_changes.why: The street needs shade and activity

floor_changes.why: The lower flats are too close to that tower

floor_changes.amount: cut the twist to about 10 degrees total
floor_changes.why: Repetitive floors keep the core and stacks efficient
Stops the flats in the re-entrant corners from looking into each other
Lighter, more slender top against the supertalls

floor_changes.why: Core-to-floor ratio is poor on this plate
Diagonal views out, and less direct overlooking

floor_changes.why: Turn the broad face to the water

floor_changes.why: Pushes the upper flats past the cluster for river views

Keep the maidan continuous
Shaded outdoor space, facing the sea

A lighter, more slender form

floor_changes.direction: one flat face toward the Thames to the N

floor_changes.direction: pull in from the S and E faces

floor_changes.why: plan efficiency and usable rooms
Heatherwick-style texture and outdoor rooms

rows.reason: A's rounded, tapered plate is more slender and more deliberate.

prob.whats_wrong: A rounded squircle with a slight taper, which is slender and sheds wind well. It is still axially neutral, though, and does not favour the harbour to the west. Among its tall neighbours it reads as a column with no skyline gesture.

floor_changes.direction: all sides, biased away from the tower to the east
floor_changes.why: a sharper silhouette and more daylight between the towers

floor_changes.direction: slope the roof toward the harbour to the W

floor_changes.direction: a corner toward the harbour to the SW
floor_changes.why: a dual-aspect water view from the corner flats
lower wind load and a softer skyline

det.whats_wrong: A diamond that fills the envelope, with small stacked shifts that read as setback blocks. It is short and deep for Midtown and is boxed in by giants. The diagonal faces look across the street directly into the neighbouring slabs.

floor_changes.direction: alternate cantilevers toward the open plaza to the N
floor_changes.why: a BIG-style pixel move that pulls the flats past the neighbours' walls

floor_changes.amount: add 20 floors within the 245 m limit

to clear the neighbouring towers for real views

floor_changes.direction: toward the Thames to the N
floor_changes.why: a skyline marker in the Wharf cluster

a SHoP-like vertical elegance

floor_changes.why: a heritage street edge

floor_changes.direction: toward the NE gap between the towers
floor_changes.why: slip views past the neighbours

floor_changes.direction: on the corner facing the docks
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space per flat is currently zero

floor_changes.amount: full lot to the cornice height of neighbours
floor_changes.why: Respect the Midtown streetwall
Twist only where there is a view to gain

prob.whats_wrong: The rounded slab is efficient and quiet, like a Piano object, but it is identical all the way up and its long faces look straight at the dense neighbours to the north and south.

floor_changes.direction: long face toward the avenue view corridor

A setback crown in the tradition of the zoning envelope

rows.reason: B turns its upper flats toward the river; A just sits there.

floor_changes.why: Activate the riverside

Street and public realm

rows.reason: A has a sculpted presence that sells; B is a commodity slab.
rows.quote: Buyers pay for a silhouette; A has one, B doesn't.

Skyline identity sells

prob.whats_wrong: A straight rectangular slab, cheap to build but flat on the skyline; its long faces point east-west, so half the flats face the road rather than the water.

Softer silhouette and corner windows

rows.reason: A is more slender and has the sea-view diagonal, though B builds cheaper.

det.whats_wrong: The slight twist rotates the diagonal toward the sea, but it costs formwork repetition, and the plate shrinks a little up top for little gain.

Safdie gardens where the sea view is

Better top proportion

rows.reason: Both are very similar pencils; A varies at the top, B orients slightly better and repeats better.

floor_changes.direction: away from the tower to the east

floor_changes.direction: toward the harbour to the west

Lift lower flats past neighbours

rows.reason: A is efficient and calm; B's expression costs plan and does not provide real outdoor space.

Make the ripple a usable outdoor space

rows.reason: B keeps the plan efficient and its chamfered corners give more flats a diagonal river view. A is a spreadsheet box.

det.whats_wrong: A plain square extrusion sitting dead centre in a generous site with the East River right beside it. rows.quote: A is a spreadsheet; B at least has a sales brochure - now give every flat a balcony.

floor_changes.why: Every flat gets outdoor space and a sellable river glimpse.

det.whats_wrong: The gentle twist through the height gives some variety and turns upper plates slightly south-east, but it's too timid to change what a buyer sees, and still no private outdoor space.

floor_changes.direction: clockwise toward the river to the S

floor_changes.direction: the corner facing the medieval lanes to the NW

floor_changes.why: Outdoor space that is also recessed from neighbours' eyes.

rows.reason: B at least moves; A is a stock extrusion.
rows.quote: B has the beginning of a sentence - I want the tower to finish it at the top, facing the water.

det.whats_wrong: A blunt square box among giants, facing the harbour but doing nothing to reach for it. No skyline identity, no outdoor space.

floor_changes.amount: sculpted terraces of 3-4 m every 3 floors
floor_changes.why: Flowing outdoor rooms and a legible sculptural profile.

floor_changes.direction: continue rotation toward the harbour to the SW
floor_changes.why: Let the gesture culminate at the crown instead of dying out.

floor_changes.amount: a spiral of double-height sky gardens every 5 floors
floor_changes.why: Outdoor space that reads as the building's signature.

rows.reason: A's rotation is more disciplined, grid-aware and fairer floor to floor; B is prettier but arbitrary.
rows.quote: B is a lovely gesture, but in Midtown the grid is the heritage - A listens to it and still turns its head.

det.whats_wrong: Chamfered octagonal plate that slowly rotates clockwise and narrows; respects the Manhattan grid at the base and gives more flats a corner. But the tiny 1,450 m2 site means close neighbours on all sides, and the rotation is subtle enough that the lower third has poor outlook.

floor_changes.direction: aligned to the avenue street wall
floor_changes.amount: hold the street wall to the adjacent cornice height

floor_changes.direction: away from the tall neighbour to the east
floor_changes.amount: pull the east face back 3 m

More corner units with diagonal views up the avenues.

floor_changes.why: Consistent unit mix and equity between floors.

floor_changes.amount: a rectilinear base to cornice height
floor_changes.why: Mediate between the fluid form and the historic grid.

rows.reason: One tower with a clear view south beats two that screen each other.
rows.quote: Make it one good tower and spend the rest of the site on the street.

det.whats_wrong: A single slender square tower, rotated to address the Thames to the south, sits in the middle of a large site. Good proportion, but the vast ground is unprogrammed and no flat has outdoor space.

floor_changes.direction: along the southern route to the river
floor_changes.amount: a permeable 3-storey loggia with a through-route
floor_changes.why: Knit the tower into the City lanes and the riverside walk.

floor_changes.direction: push the northern tower to the NW corner

rows.quote: B is the right diagram - now stop it wobbling and point it at the sea.

floor_changes.direction: toward the sea to the W and the park to the N

floor_changes.direction: lock the long face toward the sea to the W
floor_changes.why: Repeatable floors and a single strong view face.

rows.reason: Height buys the sea; it just needs a base that respects the neighbourhood.
rows.quote: Go tall and lean toward the sea - but put its feet down gently in Dadar.

prob.whats_wrong: A small square tower placed at the western tip of a narrow triangular site, shorter than allowed; it leaves most of the site empty and doesn't dramatize the sea view.

floor_changes.why: A bold, legible reach for the sea.

floor_changes.direction: facing the low-rise houses to the east

floor_changes.direction: toward the sea to the W

floor_changes.why: Give lower flats their own sky and shade from western sun.

floor_changes.why: Usable rooms at the points.
Shade the west and south faces and add outdoor space.

rows.reason: A respects the separation limit and gives cleaner outlook; B's twins look into each other.

floor_changes.direction: to the lanes on the west and south
floor_changes.amount: a courtyard-edged low base with a public courtyard
floor_changes.why: Correa-style open-to-sky space and street life.

floor_changes.amount: step rotation in 3 blocks rather than every floor

floor_changes.amount: public square in the freed space
floor_changes.why: Public realm.

floor_changes.amount: double-height verandah every 3 floors, 4 m deep

floor_changes.amount: 2 m deep balcony band every floor
floor_changes.why: Shading plus outdoor space per flat.

rows.reason: At least B attempts a gesture; A is a spreadsheet.
rows.quote: A is a filing cabinet. B whispers where it should shout.

det.whats_wrong: A plain square box rotated 45 degrees, identical at every floor. No identity on the Canary Wharf skyline, and nothing aimed at the Thames or the docks.

floor_changes.why: Skyline identity and river-facing terraces.

floor_changes.direction: toward the Thames to the N

floor_changes.direction: clockwise to open toward the river

rows.reason: A wins on buildability, B on corner views; the evidence doesn't separate them.

floor_changes.direction: a face toward the Thames to the N

floor_changes.direction: away from the tower to the E

floor_changes.direction: south-west corner toward the Thames and St Paul's

Crown in keeping with the cluster.

Shading.
